summary:
Wallis and Futuna is a territorial collectivity of the French Republic. French civil and criminal law applies locally unless a local measure overrides it, and no provision of that framework criminalises transgender people or same-sex relations. Discrimination on grounds of gender identity has been prohibited since 2012, when the statute covering employment, housing and access to services was extended to Wallis and Futuna; the term used was "sexual identity" until a 2016 amendment replaced it with "gender identity" in article 225-1 of the Penal Code. The Labour Code bars exclusion from recruitment, internships, sanctions, dismissal and other discriminatory measures on account of gender identity.

Legal change of gender marker is available under the French reforms that took effect on 1 January 2017, following the Constitutional Council ruling of 17 November 2016, signature on 18 November and publication the next day. Applicants no longer need sex-reassignment surgery, forced sterilisation, a psychiatrist's certificate or medical proof, but must still go before a court. Change of first name can be handled at a registry office, after the self-certification provision was dropped. French law recognises no non-binary status, so a third-gender or X marker cannot be obtained. Gender identity disorder was removed as a diagnosis by decree in 2010, while transsexualism remains classified under the long-term illness category ALD 31, funded by the national health insurance scheme; gender-affirming surgery has been lawful domestically since 1979.

Since 2017 transphobia is an aggravating circumstance for every crime punishable by imprisonment. Conversion therapy was banned by a law published on 1 February 2022, after passage by the Senate on 7 December 2020 and concurrence by the National Assembly on 25 January 2022; the offence carries two years' imprisonment and a 30,000 euro fine.

Marriage between two people of the same legal sex has been lawful since 2013, following Constitutional Council approval on 17 May 2013, signature on 18 May and the first ceremony on 29 May in Montpellier, and is stated to be legal in all French overseas departments and territories; registered partnerships (PACS) have been available since 1999 and joint adoption since May 2013. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status can expect it to be recognised.

Detention is governed by the French framework. The national preventive mechanism's opinion of 25 May 2021, extending an earlier opinion of 30 June 2010, found that serious violations of fundamental rights persist in French places of deprivation of liberty, drawing on referrals concerning about 40 transgender detainees since 2010 and on interviews with associations and experts. Trans women whose legal gender is recorded as male, largely those who have not had surgery, are held in all-male establishments, a documented legal grey area; one such case involved a transfer to a men's facility in Lille in 2014.

Access to gender-affirming healthcare is uneven. A 2022 ILGA-Europe report found a lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and location-dependent inequitable access, and recommended informed consent and self-determination. The National Academy of Medicine has characterised the rise in demand as epidemic-like and primarily social, urging extreme caution without changing practice. After a March 2024 Senate-commissioned report critical of youth gender-affirming care, a bill to ban medical transition under the age of 18 passed the Senate in May 2024; it is opposed by the government and has been stalled since 23 July 2024. Guidelines issued in late 2024 by the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology recommended puberty blockers with calcium and vitamin D supplements from at least Tanner stage 2.

Locally, the collectivity has a population of about 11,000, and its isolation and dominant Catholic and Polynesian norms leave practical barriers to healthcare and social acceptance. Roles comparable to fakafafine coexist with stigma and concealment.
tangentialFactors:
Wallis and Futuna has no local legislature producing trans-specific law; the legal position is the French one, and no local measure overriding the national framework was identified in the sources. The practical constraints are geographic and social rather than statutory: a small, isolated population with limited specialist services.

Provisions of French law that are not specific to Wallis and Futuna, among them the older criminal-code history, the employment discrimination provisions dating from 1985, the press-law offences created in 2004, the blood-donation rules and the position of transgender service members, are documented at the national level.

outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory documents entry or airport screening practice specific to transgender travellers in Wallis and Futuna, or local enforcement of the discrimination and hate-crime provisions. Local hate-crime statistics for the collectivity are not sourced; the French figures cited in the national material are raw counts without a population denominator.
